title: Logistic regression: why it isn't actually a regression
intro: Despite its name, logistic regression is a classifier: the pipeline is line → probability → class.
keyPoints: Logistic regression is a classifier — the 'regression' name is historical (the logit model).
The pipeline: line → sigmoid → probability → threshold 0.5 → class.
Linear regression is wrong for 0/1 labels: predictions leave [0,1] and are not probabilities.
The model learns via logistic loss (binary cross-entropy), not MSE.

sections.title: A classifier, not a regression model

blocks.html: Logistic regression predicts a class, not a continuous number — in the family tree it belongs with the classifiers, next to SVMs and trees. scikit-learn confirms it: predict() returns class labels.

The name comes from statistics: what is regressed is the log-odds \( \log \frac{P(y=1)}{P(y=0)} \) as a linear function of the features. But the output is a probability clipped into a class at threshold 0.5.
Remember: logistic regression = classification. The ‘regression’ refers to how the model trains, not to what it outputs.

sections.title: The pipeline: from line to probability to class

blocks.html: The pipeline in four steps: (1) linear score \( z = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + \cdots + b_n x_n \), (2) sigmoid squeezes \( z \) into (0, 1) → probability, (3) threshold (usually 0.5) → class, (4) train on the logistic loss.

blocks.label: probability according to logistic regression
blocks.latex: P(y = 1 \mid x) \;=\; \sigma(w \cdot x + b) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w \cdot x + b)}}
blocks.caption: Linear score → sigmoid → probability. The 0.5 threshold then clips the probability into a class label.

blocks.html: In scikit-learn: decision_function() = raw score (step 1), predict_proba() = probability (step 2), predict() = class label (step 3).

Linear regression on 0/1 labels shoots below 0 and above 1 (probabilities like −0.19 and 1.19), and one extreme x tips the whole line. The sigmoid solves both: it squeezes every score into [0, 1] and saturates at the ends.

blocks.title: Lineaire regressie vs. het logistische model
blocks.subtitle: Drag the steepness k and the threshold. The straight line (least squares on 0/1 labels) shoots below 0 and above 1; the sigmoid stays neatly inside [0, 1]. The live metrics show the predicted probability at x = 2 and x = 8.

blocks.html: Slide k: small k gives a shallow S-curve (uncertain model), large k a steep step (confident). Large coefficients ↔ more confidence.

blocks.caption: logistic regression is a classifier — see the output
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=10000).fit(X, y)

i = 5
print('predict()       :', model.predict([X[i]])[0],
      '   <- a CLASS (0 or 1), not a number')
print('predict_proba() :', model.predict_proba([X[i]])[0].round(3),
      '   <- probabilities, summing to 1')
print('decision_funct():', round(model.decision_function([X[i]])[0], 3),
      '   <- raw score z (can be any value)')

# the threshold clip itself:
z = model.decision_function([X[i]])[0]
sigma = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
print('sigmoid(z)      :', round(sigma, 4),
      '-> class', 1 if sigma >= 0.5 else 0)

sections.title: How it learns: the logistic loss

blocks.html: The logistic loss (binary cross-entropy) punishes wrong, confident predictions hard: probability 0.01 when the answer is 1 costs \( -\log(0.01) \approx 4.6 \); probability 0.99 costs almost nothing.
Everything clicks: linear in the features, sigmoid turns it into probabilities, logistic loss trains it — and the output is a classifier.
